Apologies for the long post. TL;DR at the end.

I'm a minimalist runner who recently upped my mileage, frequency, and speed pretty significantly and now have shin splints. I went from running an average of 3 miles at about a 10:00 pace 3x per week to averaging around 5 miles at about a 9:00 pace 4-5 times per week. The transition was nearly instant, and felt great for a couple weeks.

I developed shin splints 2 weeks ago. I've run twice since then- about a week post-injury I did a slow, easy 3-miler, then yesterday (2 weeks post-injury) I tried some interval work (6x400m sprints with 2 min rest between). The sprints were a huge mistake, and now the pain is constant and I can barely walk.

I saw the doc today, and she told me that I am not to run at all for at least a month, then we'll re-evaluate. She also put me on Flexeril and gave me a pamphlet on some stretching exercises, while recommending that I ice regularly after activity (cycling and swimming were recommended).

I hate not being able to run, but want to make sure I heal properly so that this doesn't haunt me any longer than necessary. I'm not really sure what I'm looking at for recovery time, and I'm looking for any advice/tips you folks may have.

TL;DR: upped my speed/mileage/frequency and got shin splints. Down and looking for advice.

I'm not a doctor but I've gone through shin splints in the past. The biggest thing that helped me was slowing down, reducing mileage, and stretching as soon as I felt shin pain. I think not running through the pain really saved me weeks of recovery. Once I realized I had shin splints, the stretching exercises seemed to help most. Can't find the video I used, but this one is pretty close to what I did. I just did it from a chair or bench in the weight room, hooked up a power band or elastic band to my foot, and went to town. Hurt like hell but once my muscles got stronger, the shin splints went away.

Oh, and swimming and biking will keep your fitness levels up without doing more damage to your legs so I'd absolutely do either or both of those while you recover. Keeping the heart rate up doing other stuff will get you back in the game a lot faster.

Along with what the other guy said about tons of stretching, I would always ice and elevate my legs after every run to keep the inflammation down.

Also be super careful of too much too soon with minimalist. I went hard quickly and ended up with a particularly nasty metatarsal injury. This little setback might actually help prevent that.

From what I've read and experienced, it sounds like you added too much too quickly. 10% increase in "intensity" (distance/pace) weekly is about what I go for. And as you've found out, don't just push through the pain.

If you can, go for 30 minute walks 3 times a week while recovering. I've found that helped me to not backslide when I wasn't running.

Hello. I was in a similar place as you a few years ago. I went from a couch potato to running 6 miles, 3x a week. Then I developed nasty, nasty shin splints and that was it for me for a long time.

Unfortunately I can't give you any advice without knowing where you have your shin splints (are they anterior or medial/post-tib?) because the location of the shin splints involves different mechanisms and muscle groups.

I likewise developed very debilitating splints after I increased my mileage shortly after I took up running. Sounds like you've gotten most of the standard doing advice in this thread and from your doc. I'll share with you what really helped me get through them:

  1. The single largest factor that improved my splints was increasing impact frequency, thereby reducing impact force. Aim for 100+ steps/minute. This is counter intuitive to your endurance, but so is pain.

  2. Choose training surfaces that are impact absorbent. If you normally run on the sidewalk or asphalt, switch to dirt or a track surface. Often even a treadmill is softer than the street.

  3. Shoes appropriate to your gait. It's a little gimmicky, but I noticed a huge difference between the hip expensive running shoes I started in and the ones that the Roadrunner analyst recommended. Less expensive too, as it turns out.

  4. Pay attention to the way your feet impact the surface. Running should just about almost be silent. A loud clap when your feet strike the running surface is a sign that you're either using too much force or incorrectly planting your feet, both of which are bad for your endurance and your splints.

I immediately latched onto your comment about minimalist. Similarly, I am a minimalist runner (VFFs).

What is your foot strike like? What do you run on?

For example, I hit with my forefoot and barely let my heel hit. I tend to run on roads during the week and trails for my long weekend runs.

Hey, I currently have a tibial stress fracture from trying to push through shin splint pain. Key advice: stop running, keep icing, and keep it elevated. It'll go away in a couple weeks. Going forward, work on your form, make sure you're not pushing off with your toes at the end of your stride, this is what did it for me. Instead of kicking off, just lift your knee.
